summary: Proposes a format for a globally unique identifier for virtual private networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A VPN runs a private IP network over shared infrastructure, and two such networks can use the same private addresses. RFC 2685 proposes a short global identifier that says which VPN an address belongs to. The identifier names both the private network and the organisation in charge of it, and it is meant to be usable by any service provider and at any layer.

questions: how is a vpn id formatted
subtitle: A short global code that names one private network, so private addresses from different VPNs cannot be confused.

tldr.problem: A virtual private network may use a private address space that overlaps with another VPN or with the public Internet, and it may span several service providers. An IP address therefore only has meaning inside the VPN that contains it, and nothing says which VPN that is.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a fixed identifier: a 3 octet Organizationally Unique Identifier for the VPN authority followed by a 4 octet index within that authority. The identifier can be carried in a MIB, in an encapsulation header or in a signalling exchange, so packets and configuration can be tied to the right VPN.
tldr.outcome: The result is a globally unique name for a VPN that works across providers and at every layer of the same shared network. The RFC defines the format only, and leaves the methods of using it out of scope.

today: RFC 2685 is a Proposed Standard from September 1999 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines only the format of the identifier, and the RFC says that the methods of using it are out of scope. The wider design it refers to, the IP VPN framework document, was still a work in progress when this was written.

sections.title: VPNs and the Need for an Identifier
sections.content:
An IP virtual private network (VPN) emulates a private IP network over public or shared infrastructure. For a customer it extends the IP capabilities of a corporate site to remote offices and users with intranet, extranet and dialup services, at a lower cost in capital equipment, operations and services. For a service provider it makes better use of the infrastructure and of its network administration expertise.

There are many ways to implement a VPN service. The IP VPN framework document identifies four types that are to be supported: Virtual Leased Lines, Virtual Private Routed Networks, Virtual Private Dial Networks and Virtual Private LAN Segments. The equipment involved may be customer premises equipment, service provider edge equipment, service provider core equipment, or some combination of these.

While the methods were still being debated, two points had general agreement. Because a VPN is private, it may use a private address space that overlaps with the address space of another VPN or with the public Internet. And a VPN may span multiple IP autonomous systems or service providers.

Those two points lead straight to the need for an identifier. An IP address only has meaning within the VPN in which it exists, so the scope of the address, meaning the VPN it belongs to, has to be established whenever the address is used. The document proposes a format for a globally unique VPN identifier that can serve that purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN runs a private IP network over shared infrastructure. Because two VPNs can use the same private address space, an address on its own says nothing. RFC 2685 proposes a short global identifier that says which VPN an address belongs to, so the same name works across providers and across layers.

sections.title: What the VPN Identifier Is For
sections.content:
The purpose of a VPN-ID is to identify a VPN, and it may be used in different ways depending on how the VPN service is implemented. It may be included in a MIB, to configure attributes for a VPN or to assign a physical or logical access interface to a particular VPN. It may also be included in a control or data packet, to identify the scope of a private IP address and the VPN to which the data belongs.

The association between a packet and a VPN can be made explicitly, for example through inclusion of the VPN-ID in an encapsulation header, or implicitly, for example through inclusion of the VPN-ID in an ATM signalling exchange. Whether the VPN-ID is appropriate in other contexts needs to be carefully evaluated.

The identifier also defines the VPN authority, the party responsible for coordinating the connectivity and services employed by that VPN. The authority may be the private network administrator or the primary service provider. It administers the VPN and serves as the main point of contact for it. It may outsource some functions and connectivity, set up contractual agreements with the different service providers involved, and coordinate configuration, performance and fault management.

These functions call for a VPN that is global in scope and usable in various solutions, so the format cannot force assumptions about the shared networks involved, and it must not be defined in a way that prohibits the use of features of those networks. The same VPN may be identified at different layers of the same shared network, for example at the ATM layer and the IP layer, and the RFC states that the same VPN-ID format and value should apply at both layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier has two jobs. It says which VPN a private address belongs to, and it names the organisation in charge of that VPN. It can be carried in a management database, in an encapsulation header, or in a signalling exchange. The same value should be used at every layer of a network, so one name covers the whole VPN.

sections.title: Requirements for the Format
sections.content:
The format has to meet three requirements. It must provide a globally unique VPN identifier usable across multiple service providers. It must enable support of a non-IP dependent VPN-ID, for use in layer 2 VPNs. And it must identify the VPN authority within the VPN identifier.

Each requirement follows from the properties of VPNs set out earlier. A VPN may span several autonomous systems and several providers, so one name has to work everywhere; a layer 2 VPN has no IP addresses of its own to build a name from; and the authority has to be discoverable from the identifier itself, because the authority is what coordinates the multiple providers involved.
sections.plainLanguage: The format must be unique across providers, must also work for VPNs that do not use IP, and must name the authority inside the identifier itself.

sections.title: The Global VPN Identifier Format
sections.content:
The global VPN identifier has a fixed shape. It is a 3 octet VPN authority Organizationally Unique Identifier, followed by a 4 octet VPN index that identifies the VPN according to that OUI.

The OUI, the IEEE 802-1990 Organizationally Unique Identifier, identifies the VPN authority, which serves as the primary VPN administrator. That authority may be the company or organization to which the VPN belongs, or a service provider that provides the underlying infrastructure using its own and/or other providers' shared networks. The VPN index then identifies one particular VPN among those serviced by the authority.

The split reflects the two requirements. The OUI part is what makes the identifier global, because it is issued to one organisation, and the index part is what makes it specific, because it names a single VPN within that organisation.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier has two parts. The first three octets are the number the IEEE issues to the organisation in charge of the VPN. The next four octets pick out one VPN from those that organisation runs. Together they name a single VPN anywhere in the world.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines the format of the global VPN identifier without specifying usage. It notes that associating particular characteristics and capabilities with a VPN identifier makes it necessary to use standard security procedures with any specified usage.

Two failure modes follow from that. A misconfiguration, or a deliberate forging of the VPN identifier, may result in different breaches in security, including the interconnection of different VPNs, which is exactly the separation that the private nature of a VPN is meant to provide.
sections.plainLanguage: The document only defines the format, not how the identifier is used, and it warns that any use of it needs the usual security care. A wrong or deliberately forged identifier can breach the isolation between two VPNs.

sections.title: Related Documents
sections.content: The RFC rests on four related documents. The IP VPN framework document is still a work in progress, and it is the source of the four VPN types and of the requirement, in section 6.1.1 of that document, to use a globally unique VPN identifier so that a particular VPN can be referred to. RFC 2684, Multiprotocol Encapsulation over ATM Adaptation Layer 5, is the example of an encapsulation header in which the VPN-ID can be included explicitly. The MPOA v1.1 Addendum on VPN Support, a final ballot document of the ATM Forum, is the example of an implicit association, through an ATM signalling exchange. The fourth is the IEEE registry of Organizationally Unique Identifiers, which is where the OUI comes from.
sections.plainLanguage: Four documents back this one: the IP VPN framework, which is still a draft and asks for a globally unique VPN identifier; the encapsulation standard that can carry the identifier in a header; an ATM Forum addendum that shows a signalling-based way to carry it; and the IEEE registry where the OUI is issued.

fields.name: VPN OUI (MSB)
fields.desc: Most significant octet of the 3 octet VPN authority Organizationally Unique Identifier.

fields.name: VPN OUI
fields.desc: Middle octet of the VPN authority OUI.

fields.name: VPN OUI (LSB)
fields.desc: Least significant octet of the VPN authority OUI. The OUI identifies the VPN authority.

fields.name: VPN Index (MSB)
fields.desc: Most significant octet of the 4 octet VPN index.

fields.name: VPN Index
fields.desc: Second octet of the VPN index.

fields.name: VPN Index
fields.desc: Third octet of the VPN index.

fields.name: VPN Index (LSB)
fields.desc: Least significant octet of the VPN index. The index identifies one VPN within the authority.

items.title: Globally unique
items.text: Usable across multiple service providers, so one name identifies a VPN everywhere it reaches.

items.title: Not tied to IP
items.text: Supports a non-IP dependent VPN-ID, so layer 2 VPNs can be identified too.

items.title: Names the authority
items.text: The VPN authority is identified within the identifier itself.
